items.title: AI Hallucinations
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has really transformed areas like healthcare, legal services, education, finance, and business. But its quick spread also brings persistent tech troubles, mainly the confusing issue of AI mistakes, errors, and misinformation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can handle all sorts of tasks, from text creation and code writing to answering questions and summarizing info. Still, despite their big achievements, LLMs sometimes spout incorrect stuff – factually wrong or made-up content – which is called "hallucination." This paper dives deep into AI failures, showing how they differ based on errors in logic, generated fiction presented confidently, and correct data being misinterpreted. It looks at why AI systems act overly sure of themselves, how messy training data messes up, and ideas for fixing this like boosted retrieval methods, cleaner training data, and humans checking the work. What stands out is that these glitches aren't just random tech snafus. Instead, they're a design quirk of big AI language models. Fixing them demands teamwork from folks in various fields, not just developers. So, while there are big issues, figuring out ways to collaborate could make these systems way more reliable in the future.

items.title: Ai-Guided Wearable Technologies and Smart Healthcare Utility in Physiotherapy
items.abstract: Abstract Physiotherapy is moving from an episodic, clinic-centred model of care towards a continuous, data-informed and patient-centred model. Wearable technologies, which include inertial measurement units, surface electromyography sensors, smart textiles, photoplethysmography-based devices, pressure-sensing insoles and smart garments, now capture movement, muscle activity, physiological load and adherence data outside the clinic. When these data streams are interpreted by artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, they can be transformed into clinically meaningful information such as exercise quality, gait deviations, fall risk, fatigue, pain-related behaviour and recovery trajectories. This manuscript reviews the technological foundations of AI-guided wearables, describes their utility across musculoskeletal, neurological, cardiopulmonary, sports, geriatric and paediatric physiotherapy, and explains how they fit within a smart healthcare ecosystem built on the Internet of Medical Things, cloud analytics and tele-rehabilitation. The potential benefits include objective assessment, personalised dosing of exercise, improved adherence, remote supervision, early detection of deterioration and wider access to rehabilitation, particularly for under-served populations. The paper also examines the principal limitations: sensor validity, algorithmic bias, data privacy, regulatory uncertainty, cost, digital literacy and the risk of de-skilling. A five-layer implementation framework and a set of recommendations for clinicians, educators, researchers and policy makers are proposed. It is concluded that AI-guided wearables should be positioned as decision-support tools that extend, and never replace, the clinical reasoning and therapeutic relationship at the centre of physiotherapy practice.

items.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Performance Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract: AI is increasingly playing a significant role in sports today, and it's transforming the way athletes are evaluated, trained, and monitored. It enables coaches, sports scientists and athletes to explore vast quantities of performance data and find patterns that they might not otherwise be able to see through traditional methods. Technologies like machine learning, computer vision, wearable technology, predictive analytics, and automated video analysis are also being applied to a growing number of technical skills, physical performance, tactical movements, training workload, recovery and injury risk studies. Such technologies can deliver real-time and personalized data to coaches to create training plans based on the unique requirements of athletes and make informed decisions. AI can also aid in talent identification and performance prediction by integrating data collected from physical, physiological, biomechanical, and psychological factors. While these are advantages, there are also drawbacks to using AI in sports. Data quality, privacy, cost, technical, algorithmic bias and ethical considerations should be taken seriously. The article will explore the key applications of AI in sports performance analysis, as well as its potential benefits in enhancing athlete development and performance, and its current challenges and future prospects.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation in Higher Education: A Systematic Review of Opportunities, Challenges and Emerging Trends
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence AI is getting more and more involved in higher education, it is reshaping teaching, learning , assessment, academic administration, research, and even how institutions decide things. In the last few years the fast rise of generative artificial intelligence GenAI, plus intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, automated assessment, recommendation systems, and AI assisted administrative tools has opened up new possibilities for universities, yet it also brings worries like academic integrity, data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, transparency, and changing professional roles. This paper actually uses a secondary-data based systematic review, looking at research and policy sources about AI and digital transformation in higher education. The review brings together outcomes from academic studies, other systematic reviews, and international policy frameworks, sort of to map out the main uses, opportunities, obstacles, and the kind of emerging trends that are starting to show up. What the literature suggests is that AI in education is not only about making content. It also includes adaptive learning, personalized tutoring, intelligent assessment, profiling and prediction, and support for institutional management. At the same time, good adoption does not just happen, it needs institutional policies, AI literacy, ethical safety nets, teacher professional development, careful responsible assessment approaches, and a human centered way of putting things into practice. A number of recent international frameworks stress human agency, ethics, AI competencies, and responsible usage, so there is a clear direction there. Overall the review shows that AI is best understood as augmentation tech with AI to help educators and learners not to flip a switch and replace the educational roles that already exist. For digital transformation a balance must exist, with technical novelty on one side and pedagogical sense together with ethical norms institutional realities and human factors, on the other. None of those should be treated as optional because leaving one out tends to break the system quickly.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Transformations in the Labour Market
items.abstract: Abstract One of the most transformative technologies of the twenty first century is Artificial Intelligence (AI) which has had a great impact on the global labour market. The adoption of AI technologies, including machine learning, robotics, natural language processing, and automation systems, into various sectors has reshaped employment landscape, productivity dynamics, and job demands in developed and developing countries. This research paper will analyze the effects of AI on the global labour market, including changes in job trends, job displacement, skill transformation, productivity gains, wage inequality, and labour market polarization. The study also explores sector-specific shifts in manufacturing, healthcare, financial services, retail, logistics, education and information technology. The method of the research is mixed (qualitative and quantitative) and the data used is secondary data obtained from international organizations namely International Labour Organization (ILO), World Economic Forum (WEF), Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. 2018 - 2025 data is analyzed to gain insight into the evolving job market as AI impacts it. The study highlights the positive impact of AI on productivity, efficiency, and economic growth, but also points to the potential challenges posed by AI such as job displacement and technological unemployment, the increasing income gap, and skill mismatches. The results show that only jobs with repetitive or routine tasks are at risk of being automated while jobs that need creativity, emotional intelligence, and high-level analytical skills are still increasing. Additionally, the paper discusses the new job roles in data science, AI engineering, cyber security, digital marketing, and the human-machine interaction. Digital infrastructure, technological readiness and the lack of training of the workforce are all challenges that developing countries have to overcome. Developed economies, on the other hand, are more likely to do so via innovation ecosystems and skill development programs. The study makes an important point about the importance of inclusive labour market transitions for the role of the governments, educational institutions, multinational corporations and international organisations.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Institutional Accreditation in India: A Framework for NAAC's Data-Driven Quality Assurance
items.abstract: Abstract For nearly three decades, the National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) has been India's main mechanism for assuring quality in higher education. Its traditional model — built around a self-reported Self-Study Report, a data validation stage, and an on-site peer-team visit ending in a letter grade — has come under increasing strain. Critics point to slow turnaround, difficulty in standardizing judgments across assessor teams, and the challenge of scaling the process to the thousands of institutions India now wishes to bring under formal quality review. In February 2025, NAAC announced a major reform: a binary accreditation outcome, an optional five-level Maturity-Based Graded Level (MBGL) scale for institutions seeking continuous improvement, a unified national data platform, and the beginnings of an AI-assisted evaluation engine to reduce the burden of manual verification. This paper builds on that reform and proposes, in concrete technical terms, what such an AI-assisted engine could look like. We outline a system that can read and structure Self-Study Reports, cross-check institutional claims against government data sources such as UGC, AICTE, AISHE and NIRF, benchmark institutions against their peers, and present the results to human assessors without replacing their judgment. The discussion is grounded in India's higher-education context: wide variation in digital readiness across institutions, obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the well-known risk that metric-driven systems can encourage institutions to "write to the metric" rather than improve underlying quality. We conclude with a phased pilot study to test the framework before any wider rollout.

items.title: Continuous Auditing: AI systems that monitor transactions in real time
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the auditing profession by enabling continuous auditing systems capable of monitoring financial transactions in real time. Unlike traditional auditing methods, which rely on periodic reviews, AI-driven continuous auditing facilitates automated transaction analysis, anomaly detection, fraud prevention, and timely risk assessment. This study examines the role of AI in enhancing the effectiveness of continuous auditing by evaluating its impact on audit efficiency, fraud detection, internal controls, and organizational decision-making. A descriptive research design was adopted, and primary data were collected from 100 respondents, including auditors, accountants, finance professionals, and postgraduate students through a structured questionnaire. Secondary data were gathered from scholarly journals, books, industry reports, and professional publications. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Chi-square analysis, Pearson correlation, and regression analysis. The findings reveal a significant association between AI awareness and perceptions of audit efficiency (χ² = 23.67, p < 0.05). Further, a strong positive relationship exists between AI adoption and continuous auditing effectiveness (r = 0.784), with AI adoption explaining 61.5% of the variation in auditing effectiveness (R² = 0.615). The study concludes that AI-powered continuous auditing significantly improves the accuracy, speed, and reliability of financial transaction monitoring while strengthening fraud detection and internal controls. Despite challenges relating to implementation costs, data security, and technical expertise, AI offers substantial opportunities to enhance audit quality and support sound financial governance in the digital era.

items.title: Current Sustainability Science Environmental Artificial Intelligence Digital Role in Human Well-being
items.abstract: Abstract The study titled “Current Sustainability Science, Environment and Artificial Intelligence: Digital Role in Human Well-being” examines the growing role of science, digital technology, and artificial intelligence (AI) in promoting sustainable development and improving human well-being. It explores the applications of AI and digital tools in education, healthcare, agriculture, environmental protection, industry, business, transportation, public services, and economic development. The study employs survey and descriptive observation methods, drawing on online information, research articles, reference books, and other sources. It highlights how AI can support informed decision-making, improve access to information, enhance agricultural productivity, assist medical diagnosis, monitor environmental changes, and facilitate services for persons with disabilities. However, the study also emphasizes the limitations and potential risks associated with excessive or irresponsible use of digital technologies. It argues that artificial intelligence should complement, rather than replace, human intelligence and decision-making. The effective use of these technologies requires transparency, safety, ethical responsibility, and inclusiveness. The study concludes that the constructive and responsible integration of science, digital technology, and AI can contribute significantly to sustainable development, environmental protection, social welfare, and the well-being of present and future generations.

items.title: Digital Transformation and Organizational Performance: An Empirical Study of Selected Indian Organizations
items.abstract: Abstract Digital transformation has emerged as an important strategic priority for organizations seeking to improve operational efficiency, innovation, customer experience and overall organizational performance. The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data analytics, automation and digital platforms has significantly changed the way organizations operate and make managerial decisions. This study examines the relationship between digital transformation and organizational performance in selected Indian organizations. The study focuses on major dimensions of digital transformation, including digital technology adoption, cloud computing, artificial intelligence and automation, data analytics, digital platforms, and digital capabilities of employees. Organizational performance is examined in terms of operational efficiency, employee productivity, innovation, customer satisfaction and business performance. The study adopts a quantitative research design and proposes the collection of primary data through a structured questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation and regression analysis are proposed for testing the relationship between digital transformation and organizational performance. The study is expected to provide useful insights for managers and organizations regarding the role of digital technologies in improving organizational outcomes.

items.title: Drawbacks and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence in the Medical Field
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an important technology in modern healthcare. It is being used for medical image analysis, disease prediction, clinical decision support, drug discovery, patient monitoring, and administrative activities. AI can improve the speed and efficiency of healthcare, but its use also introduces significant risks. This paper examines the major drawbacks of AI in the medical field, including algorithmic bias, inaccurate predictions, lack of explainability, privacy and security risks, high implementation costs, overdependence on automated systems, accountability problems, and lack of quality training data, ethical concerns, and unequal access to AI-based healthcare. The World Health Organization (WHO) has specifically emphasized the importance of safety, transparency, human autonomy, accountability, equity, and privacy when implementing AI in healthcare. The paper also discusses possible solutions and future research directions for developing safe, reliable, and responsible medical AI.

items.title: Edge AI for Energy-Efficient Smart IoT Systems: A Sustainable Computing Approach
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) is transforming Internet of Things (IoT) systems by enabling data-driven decisions close to the point where data are generated. However, conventional cloud-centric architectures can introduce communication overhead, latency, privacy concerns, and additional energy costs. This paper examines Edge AI as a sustainable computing approach for energy-efficient smart IoT systems, with particular relevance to the development priorities associated with Viksit Bharat 2047. The study follows a descriptive and analytical approach based on research literature concerning TinyML, on-device machine learning, Edge AI, and energy-aware IoT. It proposes an architecture consisting of sensing, local inference, edge coordination, selective cloud processing, and energy-aware orchestration. The paper further identifies measurable parameters including accuracy, inference latency, energy per inference, communication volume, memory footprint, and reliability for evaluating sustainable AIoT systems. The objective is not to claim unverified experimental results, but to establish a practical research framework that can subsequently be tested on resource-constrained edge hardware. The study indicates that sustainable AIoT should be evaluated not only through predictive performance but also through the computational, communication, and energy resources required to deliver each intelligent decision.

items.title: Green Intelligence 5.0: Designing a Net-Positive Digital Future through Artificial Intelligence, Environmental Sustainability, and Human Well-being
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a general-purpose layer across education, healthcare, agriculture, energy, manufacturing and governance. It can strengthen climate-risk mapping, renewable-energy forecasting, precision irrigation, biodiversity monitoring, waste sorting and early-warning systems. Yet AI is not immaterial: computation depends on electricity, cooling, water, hardware, minerals, networks and labour, while rapid equipment turnover adds to electronic waste. This paper asks how AI can be designed so that its verified benefits for people and the planet outweigh its lifecycle burdens. Using an integrative evidence-synthesis and conceptual framework approach, the paper proposes Green Intelligence 5.0, a six-pillar architecture integrating ecological responsibility, responsible AI, circular infrastructure, inclusion, human well-being and accountable governance. Three practical contributions are introduced: the GROW-AI operating model, a 30-point Green Intelligence Scorecard, and a Net-Positive-by-Design decision rule. Recent global indicators illustrate the scale of the challenge: the International Energy Agency estimated data-centre electricity use at about 415 TWh in 2024 and projects approximately 945 TWh by 2030 in its base case; the Global E-waste Monitor reported 62 billion kg of e-waste in 2022, with 22.3% documented as formally collected and recycled. These figures are presented as sourced contextual indicators, not as original measurements by the authors. The framework is mapped to SDGs 3, 4, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 16, with an India-focused proposition: “AI for All, Green by Design.” The paper concludes that digital progress should be assessed by net human and planetary value—not computational scale alone.

items.abstract: Abstract The Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly developing technology that enables physical objects to connect to the internet and exchange data with other devices and systems. These objects may include household appliances, vehicles, industrial machines, medical equipment, agricultural systems, and smart-city infrastructure. IoT combines sensors, communication networks, cloud computing, data analytics, and artificial intelligence to collect and process information and support intelligent decision-making. This research paper examines the concept and architecture of IoT, its major technologies, applications, advantages, challenges, security concerns, and future scope. The paper concludes that IoT has significant potential to improve efficiency, automation, safety, and quality of life across various sectors, although privacy, cyber security interoperability, and scalability remain important challenges.

items.title: Multi Eye disease Detection in fundus images: A Structured Review
items.abstract: Abstract Deep learning (DL) has rapidly advanced automated analysis of retinal fundus images, enabling scalable screening and grading of multiple sight-threatening conditions. This review synthesizes evidence on DL methods for diabetic retinopathy (DR), glaucoma, diabetic macular edema (DME), retinal vessel tortuosity, age-related macular degeneration (ARMD/AMD), macular fibrosis, and fundus neoplasms. We examine preprocessing pipelines, model architectures (CNNs, transformers, hybrids), datasets, evaluation metrics, and clinical performance, drawing on recent systematic reviews, multi-disease benchmarks, and regulator-approved system audits. Findings indicate high accuracy for DR and AMD classification (often >0.90 AUROC/sensitivity), promising but more variable results for glaucoma and DME from fundus alone, and emerging capability for tortuosity quantification and tumor triage. Key challenges include domain shift, data quality/gradability, class imbalance for rare entities (fibrosis, neoplasms), and the need for explainability and external validation. We conclude with recommendations for robust, clinically deployable pipelines and future research directions in multimodal integration and foundation models.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) structures rely on large amounts of private records for training and deployment. This creates privacy concerns that common fact safety systems now would not have been designed to handle, along with opaque statistical series, net scraping without meaningful consent, inferences about sensitive features, leakage of training statistics from models, surveillance, and automated decision making. The rapid development of generative AI has heightened those concerns, as fashions that are proficient on internet-scale data currently are used by tens of millions of those who mechanically embed private records into them. It assesses the main legal frameworks, particularly the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the EU AI Act, and India’s Digital Personal Information Protection Act, 2023, and identifies gaps in how they handle inferred facts, educated fashions, and enforcement of erasure rights. It also considers regulatory enforcement enjoy, consisting of actions against Clearview AI and ChatGPT, to show how current regulation is applied to AI in practice. Finally, it evaluates technical security measures consisting of differential privacy and connected knowing, along with organizational measures consisting of privacy-by-design, impact assessments, and independent audits. The paper argues that effective security requires the implementation of legal responsibilities mixed with privacy-preserving engineering, instead of either on my own, and that responsibility should be shifted upstream to people who design, train, and deploy AI systems. It concludes with suggestions for regulators, with special reference to the Indian context.

items.title: Public Health and Digital Technology: Opportunities, Challenges and A District-Level Framework for Parbhani, Maharashtra
items.abstract: Abstract Digital technology has become an important component of contemporary public-health systems. Telemedicine, mobile health applications, electronic health records, digital identity, health information systems, remote monitoring, artificial intelligence and data analytics can support prevention, early detection, referral, continuity of care and population-level surveillance. India has developed a substantial digital-health ecosystem, including the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) and eSanjeevani. WHO describes digital health as an area with major potential to improve access, decision-making and health-system performance, while also emphasizing equity, interoperability and responsible implementation. [1–5] This paper examines the relationship between public health and digital technology with special reference to Parbhani district of Maharashtra. It uses a narrative review and policy-analysis approach based on WHO documents, Government of India sources, Census material and recent peer-reviewed literature. The paper discusses potential applications in primary healthcare, maternal and child health, nutrition, noncommunicable disease management, infectious-disease surveillance, health education and referral services. Particular attention is given to the rural–urban digital divide, digital literacy, connectivity, privacy, cybersecurity, interoperability and workforce readiness. A district-level framework is proposed to connect community-level workers with digital registration, teleconsultation, electronic records and public-health analytics. The paper argues that technology should complement rather than replace human-centred public-health services. For Parbhani, a phased approach combining infrastructure, training, assisted digital access, data governance and local evaluation can support more equitable digital health development.

items.abstract: Abstract Integration of AI in the educational system is rapidly changing the face of education by offering new possibilities of personalized learning and efficient management at the same time creating serious issues related to student autonomy, data security, and psychology. The paper suggests a holistic framework for the management of AI in education by using recommendations for the responsible use of AI in various spheres developed by international organizations like UNESCO together with recent findings about the psychological state of students. We suggest that successful integration of AI into educational practices should be based on a transition from technology-based management of AI to human-based one where student well-being becomes one of the major ethical considerations.

Trafficcongestion is not only a transportation problem, but also a multidimensional urbanplanning problem that affects travel time, economic productivity, energy consumption,air quality, road safety, and social amenity. items.abstract: A smart city is defined as a city that employs communication and information technologies to enhance the entire process of governance, including making it more effective, public access to data, and enhancing the quality of government services alongside the well-being of citizens. Rapid population growth creates problems for cities associated with urban transport, air pollution, energy inefficiency, water scarcity, waste disposal issues, and burden on urban infrastructure. Smart city solutions include using new technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Cloud Computing, Big Data Analytics, Geographic Information System (GIS), 5G, and intelligent sensors, for efficient resource management. Smart city technologies help monitor different aspects in real time and make intelligent decisions in the areas of transport, health, energy supply, waste management, and public safety. In India, the Smart Cities Mission has made cities implement several technology-based initiatives for sustainable development and citizen engagement. In this research paper, the concept, design, technologies, applications, advantages, problems and perspectives of smart cities are examined, taking into account their applications in India.

items.abstract: Abstract The global community stands at a critical crossroads where technological advancement and environmental preservation must converge to ensure human well-being. This paper explores the multidisciplinary approach required to navigate global futures, focusing on the harmonization of economic science, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and digital innovation with sustainability metrics. Focusing specifically on the drought-prone Sangola Taluka of Solapur District, Maharashtra, this study examines how traditional agrarian economies can transition into sustainable models using precision farming. With over 73.96% of the workforce in Solapur engaged in agriculture, yet suffering from an average rainfall of less than 545-750 mm, integrating AI-driven resource frameworks is crucial. The paper provides factual insights into the pomegranate economy of Sangola and highlights how digital interventions can optimize water use, mitigate economic risks, and align local systems with Environmental Sustainability. Critical interventions such as IoT sensors, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for pathological tracking, and decentralized drone application systems are detailed to model an optimal input-to-output agricultural grid.

items.title: The Dual-Edged Sword of Automation: Assessing the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Accelerating and Inhibiting Sustainable Development
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a fundamental catalyst for transformation across global societies, fundamentally altering the pathways available to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This paper presents a critical, socio-technical review of AI's dual role as both an enabler and an inhibitor of sustainability. Synthesizing recent macro-level consensus frameworks and empirical case studies, we demonstrate that while machine learning architectures optimize resource efficiency, power smart grids, and augment climate tracking, they simultaneously expose systemic vulnerabilities. These include severe ecological footprints driven by the energy-water nexus of hyperscale data centers, algorithmic bias that exacerbates socio-economic inequality, and a compounding interdisciplinary 'expertise gap.' This paper maps these dual-impact nodes across environmental, social, and economic dimensions, concluding with actionable governance strategies designed to guide policy toward a balanced digital-green transition.

items.title: The Economics and Operations of Lights-Out Manufacturing: A Comprehensive Analysis of Dark Factories in the Industry 4.0 Era
items.abstract: Abstract Industry 4.0 has brought about a paradigm shift of global production systems from traditional manufacturing to highly automated ecosystems. The pièce de résistance of this evolution is the "Dark Factory" or "Lights-Out Manufacturing", which refers to a production facility that is designed to run unattended with little to no human intervention throughout the entire process. This study investigates in the secondary data collected from industry reports, academic literature and corporate case studies contexts of dark factories technological framework, their economic potential and scalable operating aspects. Analysis uses data from 2013 to October 2025. Results indicate that fully dark factories remain a niche implementation limited mostly to high volume, high precision industries; however, "semi-dark" environments are being established based on the advances of Artificial intelligence (AI), Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and advanced robotics. The study comes to the conclusion that, continuous uninterrupted production and low variable overheads cost providing the massive economic benefits to the manufacturing industries. But at the same time the management must overcome the major challenges related to the cyber vulnerabilities, large initial investments and the socioeconomic effects of workforce relocation.

items.title: The Voice of AI: Consumer Psychology and the Strategic Use of AI-Generated Voices in Marketing
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is transforming marketing communication, with AI-generated voices emerging as an increasingly important means through which brands communicate with consumers. This paper examines AI-generated voices from a consumer psychology perspective, focusing on how consumers interpret and respond to synthetic voices used in marketing communication. Drawing on literature from artificial intelligence, marketing, consumer behaviour and human–computer interaction, the paper explores the psychological significance of vocal characteristics such as naturalness, human-likeness, prosody, anthropomorphism and emotional expression. It further examines how these characteristics can shape consumer perceptions of message credibility, authenticity and brand trust. The discussion highlights the growing use of AI-generated voices across advertising, social media, voice commerce and interactive brand communication, with selected examples from the Indian marketing context illustrating their applications in personalisation, engagement and localisation. The paper argues that the effectiveness of AI-generated voices depends not simply on technological sophistication, but on how consumers psychologically interpret the voice and its relationship with the message and brand. The paper concludes by identifying directions for future research on AI-mediated brand communication.

items.title: AI Agents and Corporate Liability: A Comparative Policy Analysis for Business Law Reform in India
items.abstract: Abstract The emergence of autonomous AI agents, which can independently negotiate contracts, conduct financial transactions, manage customer interactions, and make business decisions with minimal human involvement, has ushered in a revolutionary era for Artificial Intelligence (AI). They promise greater efficiency and innovation, but also expose serious gaps in traditional legal doctrines of corporate liability that assume human agency, intention, and control. Recent events such as the Air Canada chatbot litigation, Robodebt in Australia, and Childcare Benefits Scandal in the Netherlands show that autonomous algorithmic decisions can lead to contract disputes, discriminatory outcomes, consumer detriment, financial loss, and institutional failures, raising fundamental questions of corporate accountability and legal responsibility. The paper seeks to critically analyze whether the existing legal framework in India, i.e., the Companies Act, 2013, the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, can deal with the liability arising due to autonomous AI agents making commercial decisions. This study adopts doctrinal, comparative, and policy-oriented legal research methods to examine emerging international regulatory approaches, such as the European Union AI Act, the OECD AI Principles, ISO/IEC 42001 Artificial Intelligence Management Systems, and Singapore’s AI Governance Framework, with a view to identifying global best practices for responsible AI governance. The paper argues that traditional fault-based liability is increasingly ill-suited to situations in which artificial intelligence systems independently influence corporate decisions. It proposes a risk-based governance framework requiring AI oversight at the board level, mandatory algorithmic audits, human accountability mechanisms, explainability requirements, and statutory reforms to embed AI governance in Indian business law. The study connects technological innovation to corporate accountability, contributing to the ongoing discussion on responsible AI regulation and offering policy recommendations to build a robust legal ecosystem that supports sustainable economic development in the Industry 5.0 era.

items.title: AI vs. Cybercrime: Revolutionising Phishing Detection Through Machine Learning
items.abstract: Phishing has evolved into a primary cyber security attack vector that leverages human and technical vulnerabilities to obtain sensitive information, financial credentials, and personal data. Sophisticated attacks, especially those using dynamically generated websites, misleading emails, and social engineering tactics, often elude detection by traditional phishing detection systems. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are promising solutions which can achieve automated analysis, recognition of behavioural patterns and real-time detection of malicious activities. This study explores the potential of machine learning to revolutionise phishing detection and improve cybersecurity systems. It looks at the use of supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms, natural language processing, and feature extraction techniques to identify genuine digital communications from fraudulent attempts. The study also tackles problems concerning data quality, evolving attack patterns, false positives, and adversarial attacks. The research highlights the role of AI-driven strategies in improving detection precision, response effectiveness, and cyber resilience by evaluating the potential of intelligent detection systems, thereby supporting the creation of adaptive, proactive, and dependable cybersecurity mechanisms.

items.title: Conceptual Framework for AI Enabled Learning and Sustainable Organizational Development
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to transform organizational learning and strengthen sustainable development. However, existing research often examines AI capability, organizational learning, digital innovation strategy, and sustainability separately. This study aims to develop an integrated conceptual framework explaining how AI-enabled organizational learning may contribute to sustainable organizational development. An integrative literature review was conducted using structured searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by citation tracking through Google Scholar. Thirty-one scholarly sources were synthesized according to their theoretical constructs, explanatory mechanisms, and levels of analysis. The framework integrates the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capability Theory, Technology-Organization-Environment framework, and technology acceptance theories. The study proposes an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Learning Ecosystem (AILE) framework comprising four direct propositions linking AI Capability, AI-Enabled Learning Ecosystem, Digital Innovation Strategy, and Sustainable Organizational Development. Two additional propositions identify employee engagement and technology acceptance, alongside resource efficiency and AI governance, as moderating conditions. The framework also introduces organizational sustainability indicators, a resource cost-benefit assessment, and a four-stage implementation roadmap. The proposed framework offers a theoretical foundation for examining how AI-supported learning can contribute to organizational resilience, workforce development, and responsible digital innovation. Its potential relevance extends to SDGs 4, 8, and 9. As the framework remains conceptual, longitudinal and multilevel empirical studies are required to validate the proposed relationships and assess their practical effectiveness.

items.title: Culturally Responsive AI-Supported Cancer Pain Education: A Human-Centered Framework for Multilingual Oncology Care
items.abstract: Cancer pain education aims to help patients understand pain, communicate symptoms, and follow clinician-approved management plans; however, improved knowledge does not consistently translate into reduced pain intensity. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed for patient-facing education, while evidence supporting culturally and linguistically responsive oncology applications remains limited. This critical perspective develops a human-centered framework for AI-supported cancer pain education in multilingual oncology care. A focused, non-systematic critical synthesis integrated research on cancer pain education, health literacy, cultural adaptation, multilingual communication, and AI governance. No primary data were collected. The framework proposes six interdependent design domains: patient-led co-design and cultural humility; multilingual, accessible, dialogic learning; accurate pain science that avoids reductionist explanations; clearly bounded, evidence-grounded AI functions; explicit human oversight and escalation procedures; and lifecycle governance with equity-focused evaluation. These domains constitute conceptual recommendations requiring empirical evaluation. A staged evaluation pathway progresses from co-design and cognitive testing to offline AI benchmarking, supervised usability pilots, and comparative implementation studies. Initial evaluations should prioritize comprehension, communication, trust, safety, and access across language groups. Potential effects on pain interference and other clinical outcomes remain hypotheses for prospective testing. Illustrative examples involving Moroccan Darija highlight linguistic and cultural adaptation challenges without establishing cancer-specific validation. The proposed AI role is restricted to educational support and does not encompass diagnosis, prescribing, psychotherapy, professional interpretation, or replacement of oncology professionals. By connecting health education, cultural responsiveness, pain science, and responsible AI governance, the framework provides a basis for developing and evaluating multilingual educational support. Its contribution lies in specifying design and evaluation priorities while retaining clinical effectiveness as an open empirical question.

items.title: Dentists’ acceptance of artificial intelligence-assisted decision support for oral potentially malignant disorder detection: a structural equation modeling study
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) may support early detection and clinical decision-making of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), but clinical implementation depends on dentists’ acceptance of AI-assisted clinical decision support. This study aimed to identify structural associations of AI acceptance among dentists using an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 500 dentists. Construct validity and reliability were assessed using confirmatory factor analysis. Hypothesized associations were evaluated using structural equation modeling with bootstrap mediation analysis. The extended TAM showed generally satisfactory measurement properties and good overall model fit. Attitude toward AI showed the strongest association with behavioral intention (β = 0.550), followed by AI-assisted clinical decision reliance (β = 0.220), perceived usefulness (β = 0.180), trust (β = 0.140), and perceived ease of use (β = 0.120). Significant indirect effects operated through attitude toward AI. The model explained 67.5% of the variance in behavioral intention. Dentists reported favorable behavioral intention toward AI-assisted decision support for OPMD detection. Attitude toward AI showed the strongest association with behavioral intention. The findings are consistent with the extended TAM. Successful implementation will require explainable systems, clinician education, trust-building, and effective workflow integration. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these associations translate into actual clinical adoption. Understanding factors associated with dentists’ acceptance of AI may support the responsible integration of AI-assisted decision support into oral cancer screening pathways.

items.title: Executive Function Decay: Why Managerial Judgment Fails Under Pressure and How Organizations Can Respond
items.abstract: Mental-health strain has become a routine feature of organizational life, yet managers and organizations continue to struggle to explain why capable employees make avoidable errors, why teams lose coordination under pressure, and why judgment quality deteriorates during periods of sustained stress. This article argues that executive function decay—the temporary or chronic degradation of working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility—is a central but underrecognized mechanism linking mental strain to workplace performance failures.Drawing on research from cognitive neuroscience, clinical psychology, and organizational behavior, I explain how common forms of mental-health morbidity and burnout impair the cognitive capacities that support judgment, emotional regulation, and adaptive decision-making. I show how executive function decay produces predictable patterns of managerial behavior, team dysfunction, and organizational drift that are misattributed to motivation, attitude, or character.The article introduces a multilevel framework connecting executive function impairment to outcomes at the individual, team, and organizational levels. I then translate this framework into practical implications for leaders and HR systems, highlighting how job design, leadership behavior, workload architecture, and organizational norms can either stabilize or erode cognitive capacity. By reframing mental health as a decision-quality and organizational design issue, this article offers managers and scholars a practical lens for improving judgment, coordination, and resilience under pressure.

items.title: Fear and Fun: Dual Impact of AI Anxiety and Perceived Enjoyment on Acceptance Intention of Generative AI Tools
items.abstract: With the pervasive integration of generative artificial intelligence across diverse social domains, user acceptance intention manifests a distinctive coexistence of "fun and fear." Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model, this investigation develops an expanded model by integrating perceived enjoyment, AI anxiety, and privacy concerns, whilst assessing the moderating influence of professional background. Based on 486 valid questionnaires and structural equation modeling, the model shows acceptable fit (/df = 1.88, RMSEA = 0.043, CFI/TLI > 0.90). Perceived enjoyment strengthens attitude (β = 0.324, p < 0.001) and perceived usefulness (β = 0.284, p < 0.001), while AI anxiety reduces perceived usefulness (β = -0.296, p < 0.001) and privacy concern weakens attitude (β = -0.148, p = 0.021); the core TAM path is supported (ATT BI: β = 0.643, p < 0.001; BI USE: β = 0.535, p < 0.001). By contrast, H7, H8, and H10 are not supported (p > 0.05), and professional background shows negligible moderation. These results suggest that promoting generative AI requires enhancing enjoyable interaction while reducing anxiety and privacy risks.

items.title: From Digital Victims to Cyber Offenders Children, Artificial Intelligence and the Emerging Challenges of Criminal Accountability in India
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence intensifies children's dual position in digital environments. A child may be impersonated, groomed, profiled, extorted or depicted in synthetic sexual content; the same child may experiment with generative systems, automated deception or unauthorised-access tools and thereby become a child in conflict with law. This paper asks whether Indian law protects the first child without adultifying the second. Doctrinal analysis shows a substantial but fragmented framework. POCSO and Section 67B of the Information Technology Act address child sexual exploitation material, while the 2024 Supreme Court decision in Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish adopts a purpose-sensitive approach to possession, viewing and reporting. Yet entirely synthetic depictions that do not involve an identifiable or actual child raise unresolved questions of statutory language and harm. The 2026 amendments to the Intermediary Rules now regulate synthetically generated information through user declarations, labelling and due diligence, but do not independently define every deepfake as a crime. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act's child-specific Section 9 and the corresponding final 2025 Rules were enacted but, under the notified phased commencement, were not yet operational on 19 August 2026. For children accused of AI-assisted conduct, the Juvenile Justice Act remains adequate in principle because it demands individualised, rehabilitative inquiry; technical ability is evidence, not a proxy for maturity or mens rea. The paper recommends a child-specific, risk-based AI framework joining safety-by-design, precise synthetic-CSAM coverage, data minimisation, platform duties, evidence standards, diversion and specialised rehabilitation.

items.title: Governing AI-Assisted Board Decisions: A Dual-Lock Model for Information Independence and Accountability
items.abstract: Purpose: This study develops a governance architecture for board-governed strategic decisions in which artificial intelligence (AI) provides common advice while legal and organizational decision ownership remains human. It examines two linked risks: erosion of independent human information and distortion of delegation through outcome-dependent credit and blame. Methodology/Approach: A theoretical decision-economic model is used to formalize firm-optimal and executive-optimal delegation, an endogenous attribution wedge, common-AI-induced error covariance, and boundary conditions for pre-AI information recording. The analysis treats governance controls as ex-ante commitments rather than ex-post corrections. Findings: Common exposure to an imperfect AI signal can increase correlation among revised human judgments and reduce the effective number of independent checks. Separately, private attribution incentives can move delegation away from the firm-optimal benchmark. The proposed Information Lock records designated human assessments before common AI exposure, while the Accountability Lock fixes effective decision rights and attribution rules before outcomes are known. The model also identifies limits: perfectly reconstructible post-AI judgments reduce the Information Lock mainly to an auditability device, while residual career downside can shift distortion from over-delegation toward rejection or delay of positive-value decisions. Conclusion: The contribution is a unified, selective governance architecture linking information independence and outcome-invariant accountability. It provides boards and senior executives with an implementable framework for preserving informational diversity, clarifying decision ownership, and distinguishing poor process from unfavorable stochastic outcomes in AI-assisted strategic decisions.

items.title: How university social responsibility shapes staff citizenship behavior: a theory synthesis for teaching, research, and student support
items.abstract: Universities depend on staff contributions that exceed formal duties, such as sharing teaching practices, supporting students beyond scheduled hours, and volunteering for curriculum and quality-assurance work, to sustain teaching, research, and student support. University social responsibility (USR) is enacted largely through these same staff. Yet it remains unclear when staff perceptions of USR strengthen such discretionary contributions and when they are experienced as additional, unrecognized demands. This theory-synthesis article integrates USR, micro-level corporate social responsibility, organizational behavior, and recent higher education research to explain how perceived USR may translate into organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) among academic and administrative staff. Two pathways are proposed. A relational pathway links perceived USR to organizational justice, grounded in workload allocation, teaching assignments, promotion, and participation in decisions, and then to organizational trust, work engagement, and OCB. A motivational pathway links perceived USR to intrinsic motivation, engagement, and OCB when responsibility-related academic activities support autonomy and competence. Perceived organizational support is proposed to strengthen the relationship between perceived USR and organizational trust. Eight numbered propositions (P1-P8) are developed; Proposition 7 contains two constituent serial pathways (P7a and P7b). OCB is differentiated by its target: colleagues, students, and the institution. The framework identifies professional autonomy, collegial norms, role type, and workload systems as conditions that shape these relationships. Implications concern aligning USR commitments with fair academic workload, supportive practices, and recognized voluntary collaboration that benefits teaching and the learning environment.

items.title: Innovation in Education: India's Emerging Model, Government Initiatives, Challenges and Solutions.
items.abstract: Abstract Education is undergoing a significant transformation in response to technological development, changing social conditions, emerging employment opportunities and the increasing demand for practical and skill-oriented learning. In this context, innovation in education has become an important area of discussion in India. Educational innovation, however, should not be understood merely as the introduction of computers, smart classrooms or artificial intelligence. It includes changes in teaching methods, curriculum, assessment, classroom interaction, institutional practices and the relationship between education and society. The present paper examines the changing nature of educational innovation in India with particular reference to school and higher education. It analyses India's policy direction under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and discusses initiatives such as PM SHRI Schools, Atal Tinkering Labs, Frontier Technology Labs, digital education platforms, experiential learning and technology-enabled higher education. The paper also examines evidence from UDISE+ and the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2024 to understand the realities of educational development, particularly in rural India. ASER 2024 provides evidence on enrolment, foundational learning and, for the first time at national scale, digital access, usage and skills among children aged 14–16. The paper argues that India's emerging model of educational innovation is gradually moving from a technology-centred approach towards a broader model involving experiential learning, creativity, problem-solving, digital literacy, vocational exposure, holistic assessment and community participation. At the same time, challenges such as the digital divide, infrastructure limitations, teacher preparedness, unequal access and the tension between innovative pedagogy and conventional assessment continue to affect implementation. The study concludes that educational innovation becomes meaningful only when technology, teachers, students, curriculum and local context work together to improve actual learning.

items.title: Islamic Ethics in the Digital Era: A Bibliometric Analysis
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has introduced complex ethical challenges that require critical examination through religious and moral perspectives, including Islamic ethics. This study aims to systematically map the intellectual structure, research development, collaborative networks, and emerging thematic trends in scholarly literature concerning Islamic ethics in the digital era. Employing a bibliometric approach, the study utilizes VOSviewer to conduct citation analysis, co-authorship analysis, institutional and country collaboration mapping, keyword co-occurrence analysis, overlay visualization, and density visualization. The findings reveal that Islamic digital ethics constitutes an increasingly interdisciplinary research domain encompassing artificial intelligence, digital communication, Islamic finance, blockchain, and sustainable digital transformation. Citation analysis identifies blockchain, financial technology, and Islamic finance as influential areas of scholarly contribution. The collaboration analysis demonstrates the prominent roles of Indonesia and Malaysia in international research networks, although institutional collaboration remains relatively concentrated. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies artificial intelligence, Islamic ethics, digital ethics, social media, and ethical principles as dominant themes. Furthermore, overlay visualization indicates a thematic transition from digital financial applications and communication technologies toward machine learning, digital transformation, and sustainable development. Density visualization confirms the concentration of scholarly attention around artificial intelligence and ethical frameworks while revealing comparatively less developed thematic areas. The study highlights the importance of integrating Islamic ethical principles, particularly trustworthiness, justice, accountability, and public welfare, into contemporary technological governance. These findings contribute to the literature by providing a systematic understanding of the field's intellectual landscape and identifying potential directions for future interdisciplinary research on responsible artificial intelligence, data privacy, algorithmic accountability, and sustainable digital innovation.

items.title: Knowledge producers or mere curators? A critical review of student learning and assignment dynamics in the era of artificial intelligence
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the university landscape offers unprecedented efficiency and speed, radically transforming how students access information and fulfill their academic responsibilities. However, this instantaneous convenience gives rise to a critical shift: do contemporary students remain autonomous knowledge producers, or have they been reduced to mere curators who synthesize and rearrange content from digital repositories? This paper critically examines the dynamics of student learning and assignment completion amidst the expanding AI ecosystem. Employing a reflective-critical approach, the article highlights the paradox of digital efficiency—which accelerates academic processes on one hand, yet risks diminishing critical depth, intellectual autonomy, and student creativity on the other. The analysis reveals that the relationship between students and AI is not merely instrumental; rather, it actively reshapes structural study habits, demanding a profound pedagogical redefinition to ensure that university institutions preserve the fundamental essence of knowledge creation.

items.title: Opinion Mining for Product Reviews Using Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce platforms has resulted in a large volume of customer-generated product reviews. These reviews contain valuable information about customer opinions, satisfaction levels, product quality, and specific product features. However, manually analysing a large number of reviews is time-consuming and difficult. Opinion mining, also known as sentiment analysis, uses Artificial Intelligence and Natural Language Processing techniques to automatically identify and classify opinions expressed in textual reviews. This paper presents a conceptual AI-based framework for analysing product reviews and identifying their sentiment polarity as positive, negative, or neutral. The proposed approach combines contextual language representation using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) with aspect-based sentiment analysis inspired by Aspect-specific Graph Convolutional Networks (ASGCN). The system performs review preprocessing, contextual feature extraction, aspect identification, sentiment classification, and generation of an overall opinion summary. The reviewed literature also includes hybrid BERT-CNN architectures, user/context-aware graph modelling, and multimodal learning approaches, which provide additional directions for improving opinion analysis. The proposed framework aims to provide more detailed and meaningful information than simple positive or negative classification by identifying the product aspects responsible for customer opinions. Such a system can assist customers in decision-making and help businesses understand product strengths, weaknesses, and areas requiring improvement

items.title: Personalized Use of ChatGPT and Its Association with Autonomous Learning among University Students
items.abstract: This study examined the association between personalized use of ChatGPT and autonomous learning among university students. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, correlational study was conducted with 500 students from an Ecuadorian higher education institution. Two questionnaires were administered to assess the perceived personalization of ChatGPT use and autonomous learning. The results showed a positive and statistically significant association between the two variables (ρ = 0,61; p < 0,001). Likewise, content personalization (ρ = 0,54), learning-process personalization (ρ = 0,46), and interaction personalization (ρ = 0,49) showed moderate associations with autonomous learning. The findings indicate that higher perceived levels of personalization tend to coexist with higher levels of academic autonomy; however, the study design does not permit causal inferences.

items.title: The Middle Floors: A Right to AI-Assisted Self-Representation in German Civil Procedure
items.abstract: Germany lets a citizen argue her own civil case in the local court, and she may send a constitutional complaint to Karlsruhe on her own. On the floors in between, from the Landgericht upward, every filing must come from an admitted lawyer (§ 78 ZPO). For a century this rule was a reasonable shortcut. Legal skill was scarce and lived inside one profession, so a lawyer's admission was a fair proxy for the quality of a filing. Generative AI loosens that link from both ends: laypeople can now produce structured drafts, and lawyers can now file invented case law. This essay argues that the law should regulate what a filing contains and who answers for it, not only which profession wrote it. It takes seriously the strongest objection, that writing has become cheap while a judge's attention has not, and draws a larger conclusion from it: AI should not only make litigants faster but help courts read what citizens can now write. The proposal is narrow and testable: a right to AI-assisted self-representation in appeals from the local courts, built on a structured record, a verification declaration, a court-run quality gate, an optional review lawyer and a human judge who always decides, introduced through a statutory experiment. Because a better arrangement does not implement itself, the essay also asks who would have to agree, and why they might. The aim is not to dismiss a profession but to re-examine a mandate whose efficiency can no longer be taken for granted. A right that costs too much to claim is a right in name. items.abstract: This study explores the use of digital political marketing strategies by Moroccan political parties, with a particular focus on voter engagement and the role of artificial intelligence (AI). Adopting a qualitative approach, the research is based on semi-structured interviews conducted with 16 participants, including political actors and external observers. Data were analyzed using a thematic analysis approach.The findings reveal that political parties primarily rely on social media and multi-channel communication strategies to engage voters, although these practices remain unevenly developed and largely conventional. While artificial intelligence is increasingly discussed as a transformative tool in political campaigns, its actual adoption in the Moroccan context remains limited, due to structural, organizational, and resource-related constraints.This study contributes to the literature by providing empirical insights into digital political marketing in an underexplored context and highlights the gap between theoretical advancements in AI and its practical implementation in political campaigns.

items.title: "Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Formulation Development: Recent Trends and Future Prospectives"
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is developing as a powerful tool for improving the efficiency, predictability, and reliability of pharmaceutical formulation development. Conventional trial-and-error methods are often laborious, expensive, and not good enough for addressing the complicated interactions among active pharmaceutical ingredients, excipients, process variables, and product performance. This review deliberate the application of AI, machine learning, deep learning, and artificial neural networks across major stages of formulation development, as well as preformulation studies, drug–excipient compatibility assessment, formulation optimization, process control, and dosage-form design. The role of AI in nanomedicine, liposomes, hydrogels, solid dosage forms, corneal drug delivery, and pharmaceutical three-dimensional printing is also examined. Moreover, the integration of AI with Qbd, Process Analytical Technology, real-time release testing, scale-up, and continuous manufacturing is emphasizing. AI-based models can assist prediction of solubility, dissolution, stability, particle characteristics, encapsulation efficiency, and drug-release behavior while reducing experimental requirements. Nevertheless, challenges involving data quality, model interpretability, external validation, regulatory acceptance, ethical considerations, and limited generalizability remain. Future developments are anticipate to focus on explainable AI, digital twins, automated laboratories, and closed-loop formulation systems. Overall, AI should be viewed as a complementary decision-support technology that improve, rather than exchange, experimental pharmaceutical development.

items.title: (How) Do Machines Make Sense? Respecifying Meaning in LLM-based Conversational AI
items.abstract: In this paper I revisit the question of whether machines "make sense" by respecifying meaning through an ethnomethodological perspective. Rather than treating meaning as a cognitive state or semantic property, ethnomethodology conceptualizes it as an emergent accomplishment of social interaction. Drawing on this approach, the paper argues that large language model (LLM)–based conversational AI should be evaluated not in terms of whether it “truly” understands or produces “genuinely” meaningful utterances, but in terms of how it participates in producing, maintaining, and repairing interactional order. While machines still struggle with tasks such as common sense reasoning or grasping irony and humor, they excel at one thing: maintaining the flow of conversation even at the cost of "bullshitting". In this paper, I argue that this emergent behavior, often dismissed as a failure, should instead be understood as a distinctive mode of engagement that signals contemporary artificial agents’ capacity to participate in meaning-making. A “mechnomethodology” shifts attention from how humans make sense of AI to how artificial agents make sense of, to, and with humans and other machines, thereby encouraging empirical investigation of machines’ meaning-making rather than metaphysical speculation about internal cognition or the status of their utterances.

items.title: A clinical multimodal vision language foundation model with fine-grain explainability
items.abstract: Despite their considerable promise, many current medical foundation models remain modality specific and lack transparent reasoning, limiting clinical adoption. To address this gap, we introduce Explainable Vision Language Foundation Model for Medicine (EVLF-FM), a multimodal vision language foundation model that combines broad diagnostic capabilities with fine-grained explainability. The development and testing of EVLF-FM encompassed more than 1.3 million total samples from 18 global datasets across 10 imaging modalities related to six clinical specialties: dermatology, hepatology, ophthalmology, pathology, pulmonology and radiology. External validation employed 13,443 independent test samples from 17 additional datasets across 10 imaging modalities. EVLF-FM supports disease diagnosis, visual question answering and pixel-level visual grounding with reasoning capabilities. In internal validation for disease diagnostics, EVLF-FM achieved the highest average accuracy, 0.895, outperforming leading generalist and specialist models. In medical visual grounding, EVLF-FM also achieved reasonable performance across nine modalities with average accuracy at 0.5 intersection over union (Acc@0.5) of 0.842. External testing further confirmed consistent zero-shot and few-shot performance, with competitive F1 scores despite a smaller model size. A hybrid training strategy combining supervised and visual reinforcement fine-tuning enables EVLF-FM to generate clinically interpretable explanations aligned with visual evidence. Human evaluation of these reasoning outputs using the S.C.O.R.E. framework yielded a high overall mean score of 4.25/5, supporting their clinical interpretability. Current limitations include the need for additional validation across diverse healthcare settings. Prospective clinical studies are required to evaluate the safety, effectiveness and clinical utility of EVLF-FM before routine clinical deployment. A multimodal vision language foundation model, EVLF-FM, integrates extensive clinical data and advanced training techniques, achieving superior diagnostic accuracy and explainability across diverse imaging modalities, enhancing clinical decision-making through robust reasoning and interpretability.

items.title: A comparative study of machine learning algorithms in self-driving cars
items.abstract: This teaching case examines the role of machine learning, deep learning, and artificial intelligence algorithms in the development and operation of self-driving cars. Using examples such as Waymo and Tesla, it explores how autonomous vehicles collect, process, and respond to real-time data through sensor systems, computer vision, object detection, and neural networks. The teaching case compares the functions of machine learning and deep learning in autonomous driving, emphasizing their importance in decision-making, pedestrian detection, traffic navigation, and safety improvement. It also discusses the potential benefits of autonomous vehicles, including increased convenience, reduced traffic accidents, improved fuel efficiency, enhanced accessibility, and more efficient transportation systems. At the same time, the teaching case addresses major concerns involving public trust, legal liability, cybersecurity, data privacy, infrastructure readiness, job displacement, and performance limitations in unusual driving conditions. By examining current applications and future possibilities, the teaching case argues that self-driving cars represent both a major technological advancement and a complex social challenge. Continued progress will depend on reliable algorithms, strong data security, regulatory guidance, public confidence, and responsible implementation.

items.title: A Comparative Study of the Accuracy and Error/Hallucination Types of Generative AI Chatbot Responses to Local Tourism Information Questions: Focusing on Selected Tourist Attractions in Wonju, South Korea
items.abstract: This exploratory study evaluates the factual accuracy and error/hallucination types of three commercial generative AI chatbots-ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity-when answering local tourism information questions about purposively selected attractions in Wonju, South Korea.Wonju was chosen as a local-city case because heterogeneous tourism assets coexist with facility and access information that has recently changed.Researchers developed eighteen standardized questions for six attractions, covering location/accessibility, operating conditions, and historical or unique attributes.Official materials issued by local government, public agencies, and facility operators were used to construct the reference answers.Fifty-four first responses were requested on July 26, 2026, using new sessions and a common prompt.The responses were segmented into independently verifiable factual claims and judged against the reference evidence.One Gemini response was lost due to user-interface collection artefact; because no response text remained, it was treated as missing data rather than as a chatbot error.Of 92 evaluable factual claims, 89 were accurate, yielding a sample accuracy rate of 96.7%.No hallucination was observed in this limited dataset.The substantive errors comprised one recency error related to recently changed location information and two contradictory claims involving the interpretation of historical dates.At the response level, no statistically significant service differences among the 17 complete matched items.These findings are restricted to the sampled attractions, questions, services, and collection date.The study demonstrates that domain-specific evaluations of generative AI tourism information should distinguish factual accuracy, timeliness, source-context interpretation, and collection integrity, while avoiding broad generalization from a small exploratory sample.

items.title: A Conceptual Design Framework for Integrating Smart PPE Monitoring with Proposed Predictive Analytics in Smart Manufacturing Safety Management
items.abstract: Manufacturing safety is being digitalized through wearable sensors, connected-worker platforms, and artificial intelligence (AI), but the evidence does not yet justify treating a conceptual architecture as a validated predictive safety system.This study therefore proposes a conceptual design framework for integrating smart personal protective equipment (PPE) monitoring with future predictive analytics in smart manufacturing.We conducted a structured integrative synthesis of peerreviewed literature published from 2018 through September 2026 in Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by targeted searches of occupational safety agencies, standards bodies, and primary manufacturer documentation.Search concepts combined smart PPE or workplace wearables with occupational safety, manufacturing, ergonomics, human-robot collaboration, IoT, anomaly detection, and machine learning.Sources were assembled by theoretical sampling from anchor reviews and their citation networks, and selection stopped at conceptual saturation of the framework's design space rather than at exhaustive coverage of the field.We coded eligible sources by industrial sector, hazard, sensing modality, connectivity, analytical method, validation maturity, and governance coverage against a published codebook.We organized recurrent capture-transmit-analyzeact functions into four technical layers.We linked them to a cross-cutting governance and assurance plane covering accountability, worker participation, purpose limitation, data access and retention, human decision authority, and algorithmic oversight.The resulting conceptual outputs distinguish calibrated rule-based alerts, statistical anomaly detection, supervised hazard classification, and prognostic modeling; specify candidate inputs, ground-truth labels, and validation metrics; and define controls for sensor drift, missing data, latency, false alarms, model drift, uncertainty, and alert fatigue.Numeric operational thresholds are intentionally excluded because no sensor system, dataset, simulation, or field trial was used.The contribution is therefore a traceable design framework and staged research agenda, not evidence of predictive performance or safety improvement.Future work must calibrate sensors, prospectively validate models across worker subgroups, evaluate human factors and privacy, and demonstrate that the system remains advisory relative to independently engineered safety controls.

items.title: A Cross-National Comparison of Physical Fitness, Physical Activity, and Motivational Climate Among Adolescent Girls in Iran and Hungary
items.abstract: This study compared physical fitness, physical activity, and motivational climate among adolescent girls in Iran and Hungary within the frameworks of self-determination theory and achievement goal theory. A cross-sectional study was performed among 539 girl students aged 13–15 years (mean age = 13.93; SD = 0.82 years). Data were analysed using factorial ANOVA, independent t-tests, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modelling. Hungarian students demonstrated higher performance in most physical fitness tests and had higher body mass index values (p = 0.002). Physical activity levels differed only at age 14 (p = 0.019, r = −0.18), with no significant differences at other ages. Iranian students reported higher perceptions of motivational climate dimensions. The measurement model showed good fit (χ2(143) = 1.81; CFI = 0.99; TLI = 0.99; SRMR = 0.03; RMSEA = 0.039), and structural equation modelling indicated that only task-involving climate was positively associated with physical activity (β = 0.325, p = 0.003), while other motivational dimensions were not significant. The findings demonstrated that although physical fitness and motivational climate dimensions differed across both countries, physical activity levels remained relatively similar among groups. This implies that intrinsic motivational climate may be related to physical activity participation. However, differences in physical activity levels in each country could be attributed to other variables such as education, culture, socioeconomic status, environment, among others. Task-involving climate emerged as the only dimension of motivational climate associated significantly with physical activity, suggesting a potential association between task-involving climate and active lifestyles among adolescent girls.
